description: Hi! I’m a beginner taking part in NASA Space Apps for the first time. I have basic coding skills (still learning) and a lot of curiosity about space and Earth science. I’m looking for teammates who can help with coding, data analysis, and design, and who enjoy learning together. No NASA data experience needed, just enthusiasm and reliability. I can contribute research, ideas, testing, and presentation work. Let’s build something creative together!
summary: OUTPOST 14: Lunar Frontier is a 3D, browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for students aged 10–16. The player commands a research outpost near the lunar South Pole for a 14-cycle mission. They walk an astronaut around the base, inspect nine facilities, and balance four connected systems: life support, radiation shielding, electrical power and food production. Three hands-on missions turn science into action: cleaning dust off the solar array, repairing the water recycler and getting the crew into the radiation shelter during a solar event. Every decision changes the simulation, and the student immediately sees why. For example, cleaning the array raises generation from 195 to 281 kWh per cycle. Crew needs and recycling rates are based on NASA reference values. This matters because future Artemis-era crews must think in systems, and OUTPOST 14 lets students practice that thinking through play. It runs offline in any modern browser.
details:
What it does / how it works: OUTPOST 14 puts the student in charge of a lunar research base. They move the astronaut with WASD, interact with E and open the map with M. They visit nine facilities: the crew habitat, solar arrays, battery storage, water recovery, oxygen generation, greenhouse, radiation shelter, communications and the rover bay. Each mission cycle can bring one of 12 crisis events, such as dust storms, solar particle events and equipment failures. The student responds by repairing, rerouting power or rationing resources. A single tested TypeScript simulation engine calculates every outcome. The 3D world, the HUD and the mission report are just views of that engine, so what the student sees always matches the science. Walking around never advances time, so students can explore without pressure. At the end, a forensic mission report replays the decisions and compares runs.

Benefits: Students learn by consequence instead of by memorizing. Student Mode explains things in plain language. Engineer Mode shows the underlying numbers and formulas. A rule-based Mission Advisor answers five help questions (“Why is power low?”, “Where is the damaged system?”, etc.). A Space Academy has eight short science topics, and each links to NASA learning resources.

Intended impact: To help classrooms and young learners build systems thinking, meaning how power, water, oxygen, food and radiation protection depend on each other. These are the skills future lunar crews will need. Teachers can use the built-in three-minute demo mode, which plays the same way every time.

Tools and languages:

  • TypeScript, React 19 and Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D world, with LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH graphics settings and a 2.5D fallback for weaker devices
  • esbuild, which builds a single offline HTML file of about 1.1 MB, plus Vite for development
  • Node’s test runner with tsx for 67 unit tests, and Playwright for automated browser play-throughs
  • No special hardware: it runs in any modern browser

Creativity: Instead of a quiz, it is an explorable 3D base where the science is the game mechanic. Dust really lowers power output, and shielding really lowers exposure. The low 8° sun and long shadows are inspired by NASA’s South Pole illumination visualizations. The mission report replays the student’s own decisions like a flight-data recorder.

Factors we considered:

  • Age-appropriate language and two difficulty modes
  • Scientific validity, with NASA reference values and a disclaimer that the models are simplified
  • Accessibility and low-end hardware, through graphics presets, a 2D fallback and offline use
  • Saving and loading progress
  • No real people or minors in any visuals

Use of AI: AI tools were used to help write the code, the documentation and the presentation text. All NASA data values were checked against the cited sources.
